messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Juan had always been a man in motion. As a professional dancer, he spent most of his days moving to the rhythm of salsa and merengue music. But everything changed on that fateful night when his car skidded off the road, leaving him with severe injuries and a trauma that would haunt him for years to come. In the months following the accident, Juan found it increasingly difficult to sleep. He would stay up late, trying to distract himself from the memories that lingered in his mind like a specter. The sounds of screeching tires and shattering glass still echoed in his ears, making him feel like he was reliving the moment over and over again. When he did finally drift off to sleep, he would often wake up with a start, his heart racing as if he had been touched by an invisible hand. As Juan struggled to come to terms with what had happened, he began to experience intense feelings of shame whenever he recalled the accident. He couldn't shake the feeling that it was all his fault, that he was somehow responsible for the near-fatal collision. This sense of character blame only seemed to intensify as time went on, making him withdraw from his loved ones and avoid social situations. Juan's wife, Maria, noticed a change in him too. She would catch him scanning the room frantically whenever they entered a new space, as if searching for an escape route. And when she tried to touch him unexpectedly, he would flinch, startled by the sudden contact. Juan knew that these reactions were irrational, but he couldn't seem to shake them off. As the memories of the accident continued to haunt him, Juan found himself deliberately trying to dissociate from his body, as if leaving it behind could somehow free him from the trauma. He would blank out in the middle of conversations or while watching TV, only to snap back into reality with a jolt. This strategy offered temporary relief but ultimately made things worse, as he began to feel like he was losing touch with his emotions altogether. The more Juan tried to suppress his thoughts and memories, the more they seemed to resurface in unexpected ways. He would see flashes of the accident while practicing dance moves or hear the sound of screeching tires when someone honked their horn outside. These triggers only reinforced his negative appraisals – that he was helpless, that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. As Juan's maladaptive strategies intensified, so did his sense of threat and danger. He began to perceive the world as a hazardous place, full of potential risks and unknown terrors. This heightened state of alertness only served to further entrench his negative appraisals, creating a vicious cycle that seemed impossible to break. Juan knew he needed help when his avoidance behaviors started affecting his relationships with loved ones. He stopped attending dance performances, citing "injury" as the reason, but in reality, he was terrified of being in crowded spaces or performing under pressure. His wife and friends noticed the change in him too, and it was their concern that finally prompted Juan to seek professional help. As Juan sat in the therapist's office, recounting his story for the first time, he felt a sense of trepidation mixed with hope. He knew that confronting his trauma head-on would be painful, but he also sensed that this might be his only chance to break free from the cycle of fear and shame that had been holding him back for so long.
